label: Oracle Database
summary: Sessions and processes against their limits, CPU, wait classes, locks, tablespaces
exporter: Oracle Database Metrics Exporter 2.x + a TOML for 5 metrics
source: Oracle Database Metrics Exporter (oracle/oracle-db-appdev-monitoring) 2.x: default-metrics.toml and collector.go read at v2.5.0 on 2026-10-09, where a series is oracledb_<context>_<field>, or with fieldtoappend oracledb_<context>_<the row's value in lower case, spaces to _, brackets and / dropped>; the queries were not run against a live exporter. db.cpu.pct needs 2.0.4 or later: 2.0.3's db_system carries no inst_id (its default-metrics.toml read the same day), so the division matches nothing. Five metrics (sessions.blocked, db.cpu.pct, log.switches.per.min, parses.hard.rate, deadlocks) read series that only the custom metrics file in Tutorial 15 adds (contexts blocked_sessions, sysstat and log_switches), loaded through metrics.custom in the exporter's config. In 2.x oracledb_wait_time_<class> is a counter of seconds, so it is rated; the older iamseth/oracledb_exporter used the same names for a per-interval gauge, which these queries misread. The exporter reports a TEMPORARY tablespace's used_percent as a 0-1 fraction beside 0-100 for the rest, so tablespace.used.pct leaves TEMP out. The OpenTelemetry receiver notes that a PDB connection, RDS's included, gets no v$resource_limit rows: the session and process percentages then have no series. Tools' names checked the same day against Datadog's oracle metadata.csv and the Agent's Oracle check (sysmetrics.go, tablespaces.go), the OpenTelemetry oracledbreceiver documentation.md and scraper.go, and Amazon RDS's Performance Insights metrics in CloudWatch. Telegraf has no Oracle input: inputs.sql runs the query you write, under the names you give it, so no metric names a Telegraf one. Datadog's process_limit, hard_parses and enqueue_deadlocks need dbm: true. AWS/RDS has no Oracle-internal metric; DBLoadRelativeToNumVCPUs needs Performance Insights. Host CPU (Datadog's host_cpu_utilization, OTel's host.cpu.utilization, AWS/RDS CPUUtilization) is the whole machine's, not the database's, and is not named. A ratio of a tool's metrics is null: export the computed series under the catalogue's name.

metrics.name: up
metrics.label: Exporter can reach the database
metrics.description: 1 while the exporter can reach the database, 0 when it cannot. Any 0 during the run means the database was unreachable for at least one scrape. An exporter that goes with its target (a sidecar, a deleted pod) leaves no 0, only a gap: a short gap reads PASS, and one longer than the coverage floor allows reads LOW COVERAGE.

metrics.name: sessions.used.pct
metrics.label: Sessions used (% of SESSIONS)
metrics.description: Sessions in use as a percentage of the SESSIONS limit, on the busiest instance. At 100 % new logons fail with ORA-00018; a connection pool that leaks shows here first.

metrics.name: processes.used.pct
metrics.label: Processes used (% of PROCESSES)
metrics.description: Server processes in use as a percentage of the PROCESSES limit, on the busiest instance. At 100 % a new process fails with ORA-00020; with dedicated servers every session needs one, so this limit often comes first.

datadog.note: needs dbm: true in the Oracle check's config

metrics.name: sessions.active.per.cpu
metrics.label: Active sessions per CPU
metrics.description: User sessions active at each scrape, divided by cpu_count. Above about 1, sessions queue for CPU or I/O. It is a count at the scrape, not Oracle's sampled average, so it can miss a short burst.

queries.prometheus: max by (instance) (sum by (instance, inst_id) (oracledb_sessions_value{status="ACTIVE",type="USER"${andMatch}}) / max by (instance, inst_id) (oracledb_db_system_value{name="cpu_count"${andMatch}}))

cloudwatch.note: needs Performance Insights, and is published only while there is load; statistic Average, per DBInstanceIdentifier

metrics.name: sessions.blocked
metrics.label: Blocked sessions (peak)
metrics.description: Sessions waiting on a row or table lock another session holds, usually on a hot row. Brief blocking is normal; under load it grows into timeouts. Needs the custom metrics file in Tutorial 15.

metrics.name: wait.concurrency.sessions
metrics.label: Concurrency wait (avg sessions waiting)
metrics.description: Seconds per second spent in the Concurrency wait class (latches, mutexes, buffer busy waits): the average number of sessions waiting there. It grows faster than the load once contention is the bottleneck.

metrics.name: wait.user_io.sessions
metrics.label: User I/O wait (avg sessions waiting)
metrics.description: Seconds per second spent in the User I/O wait class: the average number of sessions waiting on reads. A rise means the working set no longer fits in the buffer cache, or storage slows under load.

metrics.name: wait.commit.sessions
metrics.label: Commit wait (avg sessions waiting)
metrics.description: Seconds per second spent in the Commit wait class, log file sync: the redo writer cannot keep up with the commit rate, and every commit pays for it.

metrics.name: db.cpu.pct
metrics.label: Database CPU (% of cpu_count)
metrics.description: CPU used by database sessions, as a percentage of cpu_count, on the busiest instance. Near 100 % every wait grows. Oracle counts it per user call, so a long call's CPU can land in one minute. Needs the custom metrics file in Tutorial 15.

queries.prometheus: max by (instance) (sum by (instance, inst_id) (rate(oracledb_sysstat_cpu_used_by_this_session${match}[1m])) / max by (instance, inst_id) (oracledb_db_system_value{name="cpu_count"${andMatch}}))

metrics.name: tablespace.used.pct
metrics.label: Fullest tablespace (% used)
metrics.description: Space used in the fullest tablespace, as a percentage of the size it may grow to. A full tablespace stops inserts, which matters on a soak test. TEMP is left out: the exporter reports it as a 0-1 fraction.

datadog.note: one series per tablespace tag, TEMP included: export the max by host without it

otel.note: off by default: enable it under the oracledb receiver's metrics; one series per tablespace_name, TEMP included: export the max per instance without it

metrics.name: log.switches.per.min
metrics.label: Redo log switches per minute (peak)
metrics.description: Redo log switches in the last minute, at its highest. Frequent switches mean the logs are too small for the write load, and lead to checkpoint stalls. Needs the custom metrics file in Tutorial 15.

metrics.name: parses.hard.rate
metrics.label: Hard parses per second
metrics.description: Statements parsed from scratch, per second. A rate that climbs with the load means missing bind variables: it burns CPU and serialises on the shared pool. Needs the custom metrics file in Tutorial 15.

datadog.note: needs dbm: true in the Oracle check's config

metrics.name: cache.buffer.hit.pct
metrics.label: Buffer cache hit ratio (%)
metrics.description: Logical reads served from the buffer cache, as a percentage. A drop under load means physical reads are replacing cached ones. Weak as an absolute: compare it with a baseline run.

otel.note: off by default: enable it under the oracledb receiver's metrics; Oracle's own percentage, recorded as it is

metrics.name: deadlocks
metrics.label: Deadlocks per minute (peak)
metrics.description: Deadlocks between table or row locks in different sessions, in any minute of the run. Any is an application defect the load exposed. Needs the custom metrics file in Tutorial 15.

datadog.note: needs dbm: true in the Oracle check's config
